newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan shares suffering year-end malaise.
newsitem.headline: Japan shares suffering year-end malaise.

text.p: Investors looking for reasons to sell Japanese shares can take their pick from a variety of gloomy scenarios, some of which are contradictory but all of which add up to market malaise as 1996 draws to a close.

"Decline widens with absence of buyers," said a headline in the financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun on Friday, a day after Tokyo stocks plunged to their lowest level in a year on what brokers said was deepening gloom about the economy.

Many economists, however, were scratching their heads as they tried to explain why the market had stumbled so stunningly, given that concerns about the economy and corporate profits were already widespread.

"All the reports have been citing broad economic gloom but if you ask what sort of new news there is about the economy, there isn't any," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Baring Securities. "It's a bit ingenuous."
On Friday, the 225-share Nikkei average closed up 119.79 points or 0.61 percent at 19,690.46, after sliding more than 800 points the previous two days.
The modest rebound left the key barometer down nearly three percent from two weeks ago, and sentiment still bruised.

Foreign investors, strong supporters of Tokyo share prices earlier this year, appear not all that bearish about Japan's economy, but are fed up with companies' failure to undertake the painful restructuring needed to boost profits amidst sluggish growth, said Merrill Lynch economist Ron Bevacqua.

"Foreigners are not as concerned about the economy but they see insufficient restructuring in the corporate sector," Bevacqua said. "If profits are not going anywhere, there is no reason to invest in the market."

Japanese punters, for their part, are pessimistic about economic growth despite official assurances that a modest recovery can be sustained even as the government tightens its belt and attacks the nation's big budget deficit.

Many domestic think tanks argue the government's modest forecast of GDP (gross domestic product) growth of 1.9 percent in the business year from April 1, 1997 is too optimistic, with some predicting growth of less than one percent.
The government on Wednesday released its 1997/98 growth forecast, its lowest official outlook ever.

"Japanese just don't think the economy is going to grow next year," Bevacqua said. "As long as the 'gaijin' (foreigners) were supporting the market, they figured they could be in there without losing their shirts, but now if the 'gaijin' are not there, they won't be either."

Also undermining market sentiment was confirmation this week that the government -- as expected -- would not only stick to a planned rise in the consumption tax from next April, but would also end two trillion yen worth of special income tax cuts and postpone a reduction in corporate taxes.

"The market finally digested it (the bigger tax burden)," said Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at CS First Boston in Tokyo. "Usually people say the market discounts news ahead of time, but if anything this decline showed the opposite."
Worries about Japan's financial sector and whether authorities can pull off a five-year "Big Bang" reform plan to revitalise Tokyo's flagging markets are also adding to the gloom, analysts said.
Government and central bank officials, meanwhile, have been arguing -- to little effect -- that the economic picture is not as bad as financial markets fear.

A Bank of Japan official on Friday reiterated that the central bank believed the economy was recovering gradually and that it had become more optimistic following the recent release of some upbeat economic data.

Takayuki Matsushima, director of the BOJ's research and statistics department, declined to comment on the recent share price slump, but noted "there were times in the past when there was a discrepancy between the real economy and the financial markets' views of the economy."
Still, Matsushima admitted he had no clear outlook for Japan's economy yet. "The number of bright indicators are increasing but there are still some which are weak," he said.
